title: How Soon Can an Operator Display Show a Certified Diagnosis of a Nuclear Plant Accident? Conformal Prediction Sets on Public Simulator Data
abstract: When an accident starts in a nuclear power plant, a diagnosis aid is useful only if it shows an operator a diagnosis that is both correct and statistically certified, and if it says clearly when it cannot. We study this on the public NPPAD simulator data (315 runs of a pressurised-water-reactor model, 12 accident types, 97 plant variables every 10 s) with a random forest per time window and split-conformal prediction sets at the 95% level, evaluated on 10 random run-level splits. Before 90 s after the accident insertion, the sets were uninformative: a single accident type was shown for 9% of runs at 60 s. At 90 s a single type was shown for 95% of runs, 94% of them correct, and by 120 s a correct single diagnosis had been shown for 95% of test runs, while 3.5% were never resolved within 600 s. Coverage was 0.95 to 0.96 for a nominal 0.95. When one accident type was withheld from training and calibration, only 2.9% of its runs produced an empty set, which would show a no-match state, and 69% received a single wrong type, so the no-match state was not a reliable safeguard in this setup. The data are from one simulated plant model, 12 of 18 published accident types were usable, and no operator study was done, so the result is a bound on what a data-driven aid can certify and not a validated safety function.

Abstract

When an accident starts in a nuclear power plant, a diagnosis aid is useful only if it shows an operator a diagnosis that is both correct and statistically certified, and if it says clearly when it cannot. We study this on the public NPPAD simulator data (315 runs of a pressurised-water-reactor model, 12 accident types, 97 plant variables every 10 s) with a random forest per time window and split-conformal prediction sets at the 95% level, evaluated on 10 random run-level splits. Before 90 s after the accident insertion, the sets were uninformative: a single accident type was shown for 9% of runs at 60 s. At 90 s a single type was shown for 95% of runs, 94% of them correct, and by 120 s a correct single diagnosis had been shown for 95% of test runs, while 3.5% were never resolved within 600 s. Coverage was 0.95 to 0.96 for a nominal 0.95. When one accident type was withheld from training and calibration, only 2.9% of its runs produced an empty set, which would show a no-match state, and 69% received a single wrong type, so the no-match state was not a reliable safeguard in this setup. The data are from one simulated plant model, 12 of 18 published accident types were usable, and no operator study was done, so the result is a bound on what a data-driven aid can certify and not a validated safety function.
Keywords: nuclear power plant; accident diagnosis; conformal prediction; operator support; open-set recognition
1. Introduction

In the first minutes of a nuclear power plant accident, operators must identify the type of event in order to select the right procedure. Computer-based diagnosis aids have been studied for decades, in particular with neural networks (Santosh et al., 2007), and the need for support is greatest when the situation is unfamiliar and the information is incomplete (Endsley, 1995). A diagnosis aid raises two questions that an accuracy figure does not answer. How many seconds after the accident begins can it show an answer that is certified at a stated level of confidence? And what should the display show before that moment, and when the accident is of a type that the aid has never seen?

Conformal prediction gives a framework for both questions. It turns the output of any classifier into a set of accident types that contains the true type with a stated probability (Vovk et al., 2005; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). A set with one type is a certified diagnosis, a set with several types is a list of candidates, and an empty set says that no type fits. In this paper we measure, on public simulator data, the time at which a certified single diagnosis appears, the correctness of the displays before it, and the behaviour of the empty set for accident types that were not in the training data.

The paper contributes (i) a time-to-certified-diagnosis analysis for 12 accident types of a simulated pressurised-water reactor, (ii) a display rule with three states derived directly from the prediction set, and (iii) a test of whether the empty set can serve as a no-match signal for unseen accident types, which it could not.
2. Related work

Neural-network diagnosis of nuclear power plant transients was already demonstrated in the 2000s (Santosh et al., 2007), and the public NPPAD data set of simulated accidents has made comparison between methods easier (Tsinghua University thu-inet, 2022). Split-conformal prediction calibrates a threshold on held-out data (Vovk et al., 2005), and for classification the least ambiguous set rule of Sadinle et al. (2019) gives the smallest sets for a given coverage; it is the rule used here. Recognising inputs that do not belong to any known class is the open-set problem (Scheirer et al., 2013), and simple confidence scores are known to be weak indicators of such inputs (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017). Our searches did not find a published analysis of conformal prediction sets for time-to-diagnosis on the NPPAD data; the search was not exhaustive.
3. Data

We use the public NPPAD data set of simulated accidents of a pressurised-water-reactor model, published by the Institute of Nuclear and New Energy Technology of Tsinghua University (repository thu-inet/NuclearPowerPlantAccidentData). Each run is a table of 97 plant variables sampled every 10 s, in which the accident is inserted at t = 20 s. Twelve of the 18 published accident types are available as files with the same columns: FLB, LLB, LOCA, LOCAC, LR, MD, RI, RW, SGATR, SGBTR, SLBIC, SLBOC. We used up to 28 runs per type, which gives 315 usable runs (files with extra columns or too few rows were skipped; the type SLBIC has only 9 usable runs). The data are simulator output, contain no personal information and are used as published.
4. Method

Features. For a window that ends s seconds after the insertion of the accident, each plant variable contributes three values: its change since the start of the run, its change over the last 30 s, and the largest absolute change since the start. The features are scaled by their standard deviation in the training runs.

Classifier and splits. A random forest with 200 trees is trained for each window length (20, 40, 60, 90, 120, 180, 300 and 600 s). Runs, not time points, are split: within each accident type, 50% of the runs are used for training, 25% for calibration and 25% for testing. The split is repeated 10 times with different random seeds.

Sets and display. The calibration score of a run is one minus the predicted probability of its true accident type; the threshold is the conformal quantile of these scores at the 95% (and, as a comparison, 90%) level (Sadinle et al., 2019). The display shows SINGLE with the type when the set has one element, CANDIDATES with the list when it has several, and NO_MATCH when it is empty. The time to a certified diagnosis of a test run is the first window at which the set has one element and contains the true type.

Open set. For each accident type in turn, all its runs are removed from training and calibration, and the 300 s window is evaluated on its runs (as unknown) and on the test runs of the other types (as known), at the 95% level, over 5 splits. We report the share of unknown runs that receive an empty set (the intended NO_MATCH), the share that receive a single wrong type, and the share of known runs that receive an empty set.
5. Results

The sets reached their nominal coverage in every window (Table 1): coverage was 0.954 to 0.963 for a nominal 0.95. In the first 60 s after the insertion the classifier could not separate the types (accuracy 0.263), the sets contained 6.3 types on average and only 9% of runs received a single type. At 90 s accuracy was 0.960, the mean set size was 1.03, a single type was shown for 95% of runs and 94% of runs received a single and correct type.
Table 1. Closed-set results at the 95% level, means over 10 random run-level splits (315 runs, 12 accident types).

Longer windows were not better: the share of runs with a single type fell from 95% at 90 s to 82% at 180 s and 84% at 600 s, and accuracy fell from 0.960 to 0.899, probably because features that grow with time make some accident types look alike; we did not test this explanation. The median time to a first correct single diagnosis, among the runs that reached one, was 90 s. By 60 s 9% of test runs had received a correct single diagnosis, by 120 s 95%, and 3.5% never did within 600 s. At the 90% level the figures were 93% by 120 s and 3.9% never resolved.

The open-set test gave a negative result (Table 2). With one accident type withheld, only 2.9% of its runs received an empty set on average, and 69% received a single wrong type; for the types MD and SLBOC every unknown run received a single wrong type. Known runs received an empty set in 0.4% of cases, so the empty set was rare for both groups and did not separate them.
Table 2. Open-set results at the 300 s window and the 95% level (mean over 5 splits).
6. Discussion and limitations

The main result is a timing: in this simulator, a correct, statistically certified single diagnosis is available for about 95% of runs 120 s after the accident begins and for almost none before 90 s. Before that time, the display should show the candidate list or tell the operator that the aid has no certified answer, and the operator should follow the procedures. The result gives a plant owner a way to state in seconds what an aid can promise.

The second result is a warning. The empty set did not work as a no-match signal for accident types that were not in the training data: most unknown accidents were confidently labelled as a known type. A display that shows NO_MATCH only for an empty set would therefore be silent in exactly the situation in which a warning matters most. Detecting unknown accidents needs a dedicated method, and we did not test one.

Limits of the study. The data are simulator output from one pressurised-water-reactor model, not plant data, and 12 of the 18 published accident types were usable; the type SLBIC has 9 runs. Runs of one type come from a simulator and may be more alike than real events. The accidents are inserted at a fixed time and with the data sampled every 10 s, so the timing results are in multiples of 10 s. The explanation of the loss of accuracy with longer windows was not tested. The 95% coverage is marginal over accident types; coverage per type was not reported. No operator study was done, and the display states were not evaluated by humans. Nothing here is a safety-classified function.
7. Conclusion

On public simulator data, conformal prediction sets showed a single accident type for 95% of runs at 90 s, with 94% single and correct, and a correct certified diagnosis for 95% of runs by 120 s, with 3.5% never resolved. The empty set was not a reliable no-match signal for accident types outside the training data (2.9% of unknown runs). A diagnosis aid for operators should therefore publish its time to a certified answer and should not rely on the empty set to flag the unknown.
Implementation and reproducibility

The study is implemented in the repository articles-npp-hmi-timing: data.py (download and loading of the public runs), features.py (window features), conformal.py (threshold, sets and evaluation), display_policy.py (the three display states) and scripts/run_experiment.py, which writes every number in Tables 1 and 2 to outputs/results.json; two unit tests on synthetic input check the three display states and the coverage of the conformal sets, and they are not used for any reported result. The numbers in this paper are those stored in outputs/results.json, produced by the author's run of the script on the public data.
Data and code availability

The NPPAD data are public (thu-inet/NuclearPowerPlantAccidentData) and are downloaded by the script, not stored in the repository. The analysis code and result files are in the author's private repository and are available on request.
